docs.title: Collisions
docs.text: The collision subsystem provides 2D collision detection and trigger management. It supports convex polygons, circles, and rectangles via SAT.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
Shapes are defined by ShapeComponent:

  • RECTANGLE - four world-space corner vertices, rotated around the centre.
  • CIRCLE - approximated as a 24-sided regular polygon, so it participates directly in SAT.
  • POLYGON - N regular vertices spaced by angle steps around the centre (sides = 3 gives a triangle).
  • LINE - a segment.

docs.title: Solid vs. trigger
docs.text:
• Solid colliders (isTrigger = false) are physical barriers. They fire onCollisionEnter, onCollisionStay, and onCollisionExit.
  • Trigger zones (isTrigger = true) report overlaps without blocking. They fire onTriggerEnter, onTriggerStay, and onTriggerExit (and the collision events).

docs.title: ColliderComponent
docs.text:
Engine::ColliderComponent col;
col.enabled = true;
col.isTrigger = false;
col.isStatic = false;       // static colliders are not moved during resolution
col.layer = CollisionLayers::kDefaultLayer;
col.mask = CollisionLayers::kAllLayers;
col.shape = std::optional<Engine::ShapeComponent>{};

If shape is empty, the system looks for a ShapeComponent on the same entity. ColliderPlugin::AttachToEntity creates the collider and a CollisionEvents component.

docs.title: Layers and masks
docs.text:
Two colliders interact only when each one's mask contains the other's layer, so either side can veto a pair without touching the other entity:

// Player touches EnemyBullet and Wall only.
collider.layer = CollisionLayers::Bit("Player");
collider.mask = CollisionLayers::Bit("EnemyBullet") | CollisionLayers::Bit("Wall");

The filter runs before overlap detection, so a rejected pair skips detection, resolution, and events. Layers 0–7 have conventional names (Default, Player, Enemy, PlayerBullet, EnemyBullet, Wall, Pickup, Trigger); 8–31 are Layer N.

Helpers live in Engine/include/Components/CollisionLayers.hpp: Bit, Name, Index, kAllLayers, kNoLayers, kDefaultLayer.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
CollisionEvents stores callbacks:

Engine::CollisionEvents events;
events.onCollisionEnter.emplace_back([](Engine::Entity self, Engine::Entity other) { });
events.onCollisionExit.emplace_back([](Engine::Entity self, Engine::Entity other) { });
events.onTriggerEnter.emplace_back([](Engine::Entity self, Engine::Entity other) { });
events.onTriggerExit.emplace_back([](Engine::Entity self, Engine::Entity other) { });
registry.AddComponent(entity, events);

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Engine::ColliderPlugin colliderPlugin;
colliderPlugin.Init(app.GetRegistry());

docs.title: Querying contacts
docs.text:
auto collisionSystem = registry.GetSystem<Engine::CollisionSystem>();
const auto& contacts = collisionSystem->GetActiveContacts();

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Collisions can fire callbacks during Update. Use QueueDestroyEntity inside callbacks, never DestroyEntity. addBoxCollider in Lua reconfigures an existing collider in place rather than replacing it, so layer and mask authored in the scene are preserved.

See Engine → Systems and the Games/Collisions example.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A component is a plain data struct attached to an entity. It has no logic and no Update(). Systems read and write it.

struct Health {
    int current = 100;
    int max = 100;
    bool invincible = false;
};

That is a complete, valid component.

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
1. Data only. No getters, setters, or update methods. Behaviour belongs in a system.
  2. Small and focused. Prefer Position + Velocity over one Transform that also owns scale, tint, and physics. Systems subscribe to exactly what they read.
  3. No ownership. Avoid std::shared_ptr, raw owning pointers, and heavy containers. Components are copied, moved, and serialized; keep them cheap and value-like.
  4. Serializable by default. The editor reflects over public fields. Use types the reflection layer understands: float, int, bool, std::string, enums, and nested value structs.
  5. Stable field names. They are the keys in .scene and .prefab files.

docs.title: Built-in components
docs.text:
Component Purpose Position World x, y, draw layer z, previous-frame values, moved flag, relative (follow parent delta) Rotation Angle in degrees ScreenSpace Tag: draw in window pixels, ignoring the camera (HUD) Parent Hierarchy link to another entity Name Human-readable label used by the editor and prefabs Opacity Alpha multiplier, with optional inheritance from ancestors SpriteComponent Sprite asset path, offsets, scale, flip ShapeComponent Rectangle, circle, regular polygon, or line Text String, font, size, spacing, colour CameraComponent Zoom, follow target, bounds, shake ColliderComponent Collision shape and layer/mask CollisionEvents Callbacks for collision and trigger lifecycle AudioSource Sound or music request Input Per-entity action state and player index ScriptComponent Lua script path and runtime state PrefabInstance Link back to the prefab that spawned this entity SignalConnections Subscriptions to typed signals NetworkComponent Replication flags and network identity PluginExampleEvents Example event component from the plugin sample

Most of these have dedicated pages: Rendering, Collisions, Audio, Input, Networking, Scripting.

docs.title: Tags are components too
docs.text:
A component with no fields is a tag. It carries one bit of information: "this entity is different".

struct PlayerTag {};
registry.AddComponent(player, PlayerTag{});

ScreenSpace is the built-in example: the renderer checks for it and switches to the HUD pass. Use tags instead of booleans on unrelated components; they compose better.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text: Components opt into serialization through Engine/include/Reflection/ComponentReflect.hpp. If a component is missing there, the editor cannot save it. See Scene format.

docs.title: Notes on Transform
docs.text: The engine does not have a Transform component. It uses separate Position and Rotation components, plus Parent for hierarchy. When porting snippets, replace Transform{ .x, .y } with Position(x, y).

docs.title: Headless mode
docs.text: Headless mode runs the engine without a window or rendering. Systems and networking still tick, which is how the multiplayer server runs.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
Set config.headless = true:

Engine::ApplicationConfig config;
config.headless = true;
Engine::Application app(config);
app.Run();

Or pass --headless to a generated game, which MultiplayerPlugin reads from the launch options.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
• InitWindow is not called; no OpenGL context is created.
  • VirtualResolution is not registered, so there is no canvas.
  • PostUpdate returns immediately: no rendering, no onUI.
  • PreUpdate skips virtual-canvas scaling and mouse mapping, but still polls input.
  • Update runs every registered system in order, including ScriptSystem and MultiplayerSystem.

docs.title: What stays the same
docs.text:
• The fixed timestep loop and dt.
  • Component, system, and resource registration.
  • Scene loading through SceneManager.
  • Networking: the server host is created and polls every tick.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Dedicated multiplayer servers (Game --server --headless).
  • Automated tests that exercise gameplay without a window.
  • Batch processing or headless simulation.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Systems that assume a window (rendering, ImGui) must guard with HasResource<VirtualResolution>().
  • GetGameTexture() throws ErrorEcs in headless mode because the resource is missing.
  • Audio may still open a device; disable it by skipping AudioPlugin::Init() if you do not need sound on a server.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: The input system is hardware-agnostic and dynamic. You bind string actions to physical keys, mouse buttons, or gamepad buttons at runtime, and gameplay reads actions by name.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Engine::InputPlugin inputPlugin;
inputPlugin.Init(app.GetRegistry());

auto& inputManager = app.GetRegistry().GetResource<Engine::InputManager>();
inputManager.AddPlayer(1, std::make_unique<Engine::Controller>());
auto* p1 = inputManager.GetController(1);

if (p1) {
    p1->addKeybind("MOVE_UP", {KEY_W, 0, Engine::KEYBOARD});
    p1->addKeybind("MOVE_UP", {KEY_UP, 0, Engine::KEYBOARD});
    p1->addKeybind("SHOOT", {KEY_SPACE, 0, Engine::KEYBOARD});
    p1->addKeybind("SHOOT", {MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT, 0, Engine::MOUSE});
    p1->addKeybind("SHOOT", {GAMEPAD_BUTTON_RIGHT_FACE_DOWN, 0, Engine::GAMEPAD});
}

Controller polls Raylib keyboard, mouse, and gamepad APIs. Subclass IController to feed actions from a network packet or a custom device.

docs.title: Attaching input to entities
docs.text:
Engine::Entity player = registry.CreateEntity();
Engine::InputPlugin::AttachToEntity(registry, player, 1);

The Input component has playerIdx and isActive. Set isActive = false to ignore input for an entity during cutscenes or stuns.

docs.title: Reading input in a system
docs.text:
class MovementSystem : public Engine::System {
  public:
    void Update(Engine::Registry& registry, float dt) override {
        if (!registry.HasResource<Engine::InputManager>()) return;
        auto& inputManager = registry.GetResource<Engine::InputManager>();

        for (auto& [entity, input] : *registry.GetComponentArray<Engine::Input>()) {
            if (!input.isActive) continue;
            auto* controller = inputManager.GetController(input.playerIdx);
            if (!controller) continue;

            auto& pos = registry.RequireComponent<Engine::Position>(entity);
            if (controller->isActionActive("MOVE_UP"))    pos.y -= 250.0f * dt;
            if (controller->isActionActive("MOVE_DOWN"))   pos.y += 250.0f * dt;
            if (controller->isActionActive("MOVE_LEFT"))   pos.x -= 250.0f * dt;
            if (controller->isActionActive("MOVE_RIGHT"))  pos.x += 250.0f * dt;
        }
    }
};

docs.title: Multi-player
docs.text: Add more players with inputManager.AddPlayer(2, std::make_unique<Engine::Controller>(1)). In multiplayer, the client sends input to the server; the server simulates. See Networking.

docs.title: Input mapping in the editor
docs.text: The editor stores actions and keybinds in input.json and provides the Input Map panel for editing them without code. The map is baked into the game launcher, so changing it requires a rebuild.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Engine and editor code record messages with the macros in Logging/Logger.hpp. The caller does not write to the terminal itself.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
log_error, log_debug, log_info, and log_user_error move the line onto a queue and return. One background thread writes the batch, then flushes. [ERROR] goes to standard error. [DEBUG] and [INFO] go to standard output.

That thread is per process. A game started with Play has its own writer. Those lines stay on that process's terminal. They are not piped into the editor.

The web build has no worker thread. There, each line is written on the caller.

docs.title: Editor Console
docs.text:
The Console panel lists user problems only. A line appears there when code calls log_user_error. That is a failure of something the user controls: a script, a prefab, a scene file, a path, or a drag that the hierarchy rejects.

log_error, log_debug, and log_info are engine and editor diagnostics. They stay on the terminal. An empty Console means there is no user problem to show.

docs.title: Lua
docs.text:
Scripts use the log table and the global print.

Call Where it shows log.error("...") Editor Console and the terminal log.info("...") Terminal only log.debug("...") Terminal only print(...) Terminal only 
log.error("missing player spawn")
log.info("wave started")
print("tick", 3)

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Multiplayer in this engine is server-authoritative. That is a fancy way of saying: one machine is the referee, everyone else is a player. The referee owns the board and decides what is true. Players may only say "I press left". The referee moves the piece and announces where everything is. Nobody moves their own piece on their own board.

That single idea explains why two players see the same world, and why cheating by editing your own copy does nothing.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Every process is in exactly one role, decided at startup.

Role Who simulates the world Sends Applies Single-player this process nothing nothing Server this process (authoritative) spawn / state / despawn - Client nobody, for networked entities input spawn / state / despawn

A single-player game is not "multiplayer with one player". There is no host at all, and replication does nothing. This is on purpose: a single-player build never pays for networking it does not use, and one script can support all three modes by checking Net.isNetworked().

docs.title: Choosing a role
docs.text:
Game                       # single-player
Game --server              # server on port 3000
Game --server --port 4000  # server on another port
Game --server --headless   # server with no window
Game --client              # connect to 127.0.0.1:3000
Game --client --host 10.0.0.5 --port 4000

With no flag, no host is created and the scene runs exactly as before. The editor's Play Multiplayer button launches these commands for you, so you do not need a terminal.

ENet is initialised lazily and exactly once inside NetworkHostResource. You never call enet_initialize yourself.

docs.title: The only thing you write: NetworkComponent
docs.text:
Tag an entity with a NetworkComponent and the engine handles identity, spawning, input, and state sync.

Field Type Meaning networkId uint64_t Engine-assigned identity. 0 means "not assigned yet". Never serialized. authority string "Server", "Client", or "Shared" (see below). syncTransform bool Sync Position + Rotation every tick. syncSprite bool Sync the SpriteComponent (path, offsets, scale, flips). prefabPath string Project-relative prefab to instantiate on the other machine.

docs.title: Authority, in plain words
docs.text:
• Server: the server simulates it; clients follow. Enemies, pickups, platforms.
  • Client: one client sends input; the server still simulates it. Each connected player. This is the one that trips people up: "Client" does not mean "the client simulates this". The client only contributes input; the server runs the movement and broadcasts the result.
  • Shared: not synced at all; built identically from the scene. Walls, background.

There is no "both". If both machines simulated one entity, they would disagree the moment anything non-deterministic happened, and the next snapshot would snap the loser back. That rubber-banding is exactly what authority exists to prevent.

docs.title: How your script stays one file
docs.text:
Every replicated script guards its movement with the same predicate:

local function shouldSimulate()
    if not Net.isNetworked() then return true end   -- single-player: I am the only machine
    return Net.isServer()                          -- multiplayer: only the server simulates
end

One script, three outcomes:

Process Net.isNetworked() Net.isServer() shouldSimulate() Single-player false false true Server true true true Client true false false

A client script is not useless: it still runs onCreate / onDestroy, RPC handlers, and purely local effects (a muzzle flash, a HUD update). It only skips the part that decides the entity's position.

docs.title: Frame order, and why it matters
docs.text:
Script runs before Replication, so Lua moves the player first and Replication broadcasts the new position in the same tick. Multiplayer (the ENet poll) runs last, so packets received this tick are dispatched immediately.

ReplicationPlugin must register before MultiplayerPlugin, otherwise the very first poll could deliver a packet to a router with no handler yet.

docs.title: The plumbing (short version)
docs.text:
• NetworkHostResource is the only class that knows about ENet.
  • PacketRegistryResource hashes packet names to deterministic 16-bit ids, so a Windows client and a Linux server agree on "replication_spawn" without sharing a table.
  • PacketRouterResource dispatches packets to handlers.
  • PrefabSpawner is a function pointer installed by the serializer, used to spawn prefabs at runtime on the server and clients.

Packets are [2 bytes id, little-endian][payload]. Spawns, despawns, and identity are reliable; state and input are unreliable because the next snapshot supersedes them.

docs.title: Limits (read these before designing)
docs.text:
• Maximum 5 connected players.
  • No client-side prediction: clients do not move their own player locally, so there is a tick of latency.
  • No prefab instantiation from Lua; the engine spawns players.
  • Clients follow the server's scene loads; their own Scene.load calls are ignored.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: Set RTYPE_NET_DEBUG=1 for a process to log per-second input and position lines.

docs.title: Lua API
docs.text: Scripts use the Net namespace: isNetworked, isServer, isLocal, localId, playerSlot, replicate, rpc, rpcUnreliable, broadcast, on, off, register, onConnect, onDisconnect, send, input, and more. See Reference → Net.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Editor → Multiplayer - the launch workflow.
  • How do I...? → Add multiplayer.
  • Lua cookbook.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text: Engine::Registry is the coordinator of the ECS. It owns entity allocation, component storage, system registration and ordering, and global resources.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
An Engine::Entity is a std::size_t, an identifier with no data. CreateEntity() allocates a new id and attaches a default Position and Rotation:

Engine::Entity player = registry.CreateEntity();

Destroying an entity destroys its descendants (anything whose Parent points at it). Two forms exist:

registry.DestroyEntity(enemy);         // immediate
registry.QueueDestroyEntity(enemy);    // deferred to FlushQueues

Always queue from gameplay code. QueueDestroyEntity records the request and FlushQueues runs it at the end of the frame, so iterating a component array never gets invalidated mid-loop. Immediate destruction is for editor and tooling code.

ClearEntities() removes every entity and restarts ids at 1, while keeping component types, systems, and resources registered. It is used when switching scenes.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Register before use:

registry.RegisterComponent<Health>();

Position, Rotation, and ScreenSpace are registered by the registry itself; plugins register the rest.

Add, read, and remove:

registry.AddComponent(enemy, Engine::Health{ .current = 3, .max = 3 });

bool has = registry.HasComponent<Engine::Health>(enemy);
auto& health = registry.RequireComponent<Engine::Health>(enemy); // throws ErrorEcs if missing

std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<Engine::Health>> maybe =
    registry.GetComponent<Engine::Health>(enemy); // nullopt when absent

registry.RemoveComponent<Engine::Health>(enemy);

AddComponent inserts or replaces. The component array is a std::unordered_map<Entity, T> per type, so iteration is cache-friendly relative to the number of entities of that type.

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
Register in dependency order:

auto system = registry.RegisterSystem<MovementSystem>(); // returns shared_ptr<T>

RegisterSystem<T>() returns a std::shared_ptr<T> so you can configure the system afterwards. Registration order is update order and render order. Look up a registered system with GetSystem<T>().

OnSceneUnloaded(Registry&) is called on each system right before the scene's entities are destroyed, so systems can drop state kept outside components.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Global, one-per-game data:

auto& assets = registry.AddResource<Engine::AssetManager>();
auto& input  = registry.GetResource<Engine::InputManager>(); // throws if missing
bool has     = registry.HasResource<Engine::InputManager>();

Use resources for things that are one per game (asset tables, input state, network host) and components for things that are one per entity.

docs.title: Iteration
docs.text:
for (auto& [entity, position] : *registry.GetComponentArray<Engine::Position>()) {
    position.x += 100.0f * dt;
}

GetComponentArray<T>() throws ErrorEcs if T was never registered. Checking several components means a HasComponent per entity; there is no query language.

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
• Keep components dumb: no methods, no owning pointers.
  • Never destroy an entity directly while iterating; queue it.
  • Register systems deliberately; the order is the update order.
  • Bundle registration in a plugin when a feature needs a component, a system, and a resource.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
The renderer draws the registry in two passes every frame: a world pass inside the active camera, then a screen pass in window pixels for HUD elements. Entities tagged ScreenSpace are drawn in the screen pass; everything else in the world pass.

Within each pass, layered systems (sprites, shapes, text) draw first, sorted by Position::z, then by system registration order, then by entity id. Non-layered systems then run their Render / RenderScreen in registration order.

docs.title: Sprites
docs.text:
SpriteComponent names an asset and places it relative to the entity:

Engine::SpriteComponent sprite;
sprite.assetPath = "assets/player.png";
sprite.offsetX = -12.8f;
sprite.offsetY = -14.0f;
sprite.scaleX = 4.0f;
sprite.scaleY = 4.0f;
sprite.flipX = false;
sprite.flipY = false;

The sprite's top-left corner is drawn at (Position.x + offsetX, Position.y + offsetY). Positions are top-left corners everywhere in the engine, which is why the offset is what centres a padded sprite on its collider. SpriteSystem reads Rotation from the same entity and applies scaleX/scaleY when drawing.

Flipping is visual only: flipX/flipY mirror the drawing about the sprite's own centre. Component.flipX(entity) (Lua) also mirrors the whole child subtree about the entity's centre, so a rig turns around in one call.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
ShapeComponent supports rectangles, circles, regular polygons, and lines:

Engine::ShapeComponent body;
body.type = Engine::ShapeType::RECTANGLE;
body.width = 48.0f;
body.height = 32.0f;
body.color = SKYBLUE;
body.filled = true;

For polygons, set sides and radius. For lines, set endOffset and thickness.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
TextPlugin registers Text and TextSystem. Attach text with:

Engine::TextPlugin::AttachToEntity(registry, entity, "Score: 0", 24.0f);

Custom fonts, colours, and spacing are set directly on the Text component. If font.texture.id == 0 (no custom font loaded), the system falls back to Raylib's built-in font. Entities without a Position are skipped safely.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
A camera is a normal entity with a CameraComponent and a Position. The active camera is the one with primary = true and the lowest entity id. CameraSystem handles follow, bounds, zoom, rotation, and shake.

Engine::CameraComponent cam;
cam.followTarget = player;
cam.followSpeed = 5.0f;       // 0 snaps instantly
cam.clampToBounds = true;
cam.bounds = {0.0f, 0.0f, levelWidth, levelHeight};
cam.zoom = 2.0f;
cam.shakeTrauma = 1.0f;       // shake strength is magnitude * trauma^2

Shake is visual only and never moves the camera's Position. The clamp ignores rotation.

HUD elements use the ScreenSpace tag and are drawn in window pixels. Convert between screen and world coordinates with CameraSystem::ScreenToWorld and WorldToScreen.

docs.title: Virtual resolution
docs.text: VirtualResolution is a fixed-size game canvas scaled and centred into the OS window with letterboxing or pillarboxing. The mouse can be mapped back into canvas space. Set virtualWidth/virtualHeight in ApplicationConfig; 0 means match the window.

docs.title: Virtual canvas and editor
docs.text:
The editor's Scene view renders the registry with the same systems and camera, at the project's virtual resolution, so what you see is what the game draws. The editor camera is separate and can be panned and zoomed without affecting the game camera.

See Camera in the old guides and Engine → Assets.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Resources are global, one-per-game values shared between systems: asset tables, input state, the network host, project paths, scene management. They are not attached to entities.

docs.title: Adding and reading
docs.text:
auto& assets = registry.AddResource<Engine::AssetManager>();
auto& input  = registry.GetResource<Engine::InputManager>(); // throws if missing
bool has     = registry.HasResource<Engine::InputManager>();

AddResource<T>(args...) constructs in place and returns a reference. GetResource<T>() throws ErrorEcs if the resource is missing. Guard shared resources with HasResource<T>() inside plugins so two plugins do not add the same one twice.

docs.title: Built-in resources
docs.text: Resource Provided by Purpose AssetManager SpritePlugin / AudioPlugin Loaded sprites, sounds, music, fonts InputManager InputPlugin Controller instances per player VirtualResolution Application Virtual canvas and letterboxing LaunchOptions Application Command-line arguments ProjectContext Editor / scene loading Project folder and path resolution SceneManager Scene loading Pending scene switch requests State<T> / NextState<T> / StateTransitionEvent<T> User State machine state NetworkHostResource MultiplayerPlugin ENet host and polling PacketRegistryResource MultiplayerPlugin Deterministic packet name-to-id map PacketRouterResource MultiplayerPlugin Packet id-to-handler dispatch PlayerInputState MultiplayerPlugin Server-side network id to last input PlayerSlotState MultiplayerPlugin Network id to color slot (max 5) PrefabSpawner Serialization::SceneSerializer Runtime prefab instantiation hook EditorMode Editor Tag resource that keeps ScriptSystem idle in the editor

docs.title: Component vs. resource
docs.text: Use a component for anything that is one per entity (position, health, sprite). Use a resource for anything that is one per game (asset table, input state, network host). A system can read both in the same frame.

docs.title: Lua scripting
docs.text:
The engine exposes gameplay scripting through ScriptComponent and ScriptSystem, using sol2. A script returns a table with optional lifecycle functions:

local Enemy = {}

function Enemy:onCreate(entity)
    self.entity = entity
end

function Enemy:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    -- runs every frame
end

function Enemy:onDestroy(entity)
    -- runs when the entity is destroyed
end

return Enemy

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Engine::ScriptPlugin scriptPlugin;
scriptPlugin.Init(app.GetRegistry());

ScriptPlugin registers ScriptComponent and ScriptSystem. Attach a script:

registry.AddComponent(entity, Engine::ScriptComponent("scripts/enemy.lua"));

Or use the helper:

Engine::ScriptPlugin::AttachToEntity(registry, entity, Engine::ScriptComponent("scripts/enemy.lua"));

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• onCreate(entity) - once, when the script is loaded.
  • onUpdate(entity, dt) - every frame, with dt in seconds.
  • onDestroy(entity) - when the entity is destroyed.
  • onCollisionEnter/Stay/Exit(this, other) - collision callbacks, when connected.

The editor does not run Lua. Scripts only execute in the game process started by Play.

docs.title: Auto-reload
docs.text: ScriptComponent::autoReload (default true) reloads the script when the file changes on disk. There is no hot reload in the running process; save the file, close the game window, and click Play again.

docs.title: Engine API
docs.text:
Scripts use the global namespaces registered by LuaAPI:

  • Entity - create, destroy, queueDestroy, find, getName, setName
  • Transform - getPosition, setPosition, translate, getZIndex, setZIndex, getRotation, setRotation, rotate
  • Component - addSprite, getSprite, addShape, addText, addBoxCollider, flipX, flipY, setSpritePath, setParent, getChildren, and many more
  • Input - isKeyDown, isKeyPressed, isKeyReleased, getMousePosition, plus KEY.*
  • Controller - isActionActive, getActiveActions, addKeybind, hasController, plus Controller.KEYBOARD.*
  • Time - Time.time, Time.deltaTime
  • Net - register, on, off, send, broadcast, onConnect, onDisconnect, isServer, localId, replicate, rpc, and more
  • Scene - Scene.load(name), Scene.current()
  • log / print - logging at info/warn/error/debug levels

See Reference → Lua API for the full list.

docs.title: ScriptComponent fields
docs.text: Field Default Notes scriptPath empty Path relative to the project folder autoReload true Reload when the file changes loaded false Internal: whether the script loaded successfully scriptTable nil Internal: sol2 table handle

docs.title: Networking and scripts
docs.text: In multiplayer, guard simulation with Net.isNetworked() and Net.isServer() so the same script runs in single-player, on the server, and on clients without changes. See Networking.

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
A system is where behaviour lives. It reads and writes components, once per fixed step, for every entity that has the data it cares about.

Components are passive (Components); systems are the only place where values change.

docs.title: The System interface
docs.text:
Every system inherits from Engine::System and overrides the passes it needs:

#include "ECS/System.hpp"

class MovementSystem : public Engine::System {
  public:
    void Update(Engine::Registry& registry, float dt) override {
        for (auto& [entity, position] : *registry.GetComponentArray<Engine::Position>()) {
            position.x += 120.0f * dt;
        }
    }
};

The three passes run in this order every frame:

Pass Signature Environment Typical use Update Update(Registry&, float dt) Before rendering Simulate, poll input, resolve collisions Render Render(Registry&) Inside the active camera World-space drawing RenderScreen RenderScreen(Registry&) Window pixels, no camera HUD, menus, overlays

dt is the frame delta in seconds. Multiply everything time-based by it. OnSceneUnloaded is called right before a scene's entities are destroyed, so systems can drop state kept outside components.

docs.title: Registering a system
docs.text:
auto movement = registry.RegisterSystem<MovementSystem>(); // shared_ptr<T>

Registration order is update order. If system B reads data written by system A, register A first:

registry.RegisterSystem<HierarchySystem>();   // first: propagate parent motion
registry.RegisterSystem<PositionSystem>();    // then: snapshot previous positions

RegisterSystem<T>() returns a std::shared_ptr<T> if you need to configure the system afterwards.

docs.title: Iterating entities
docs.text:
Over one component array:

for (auto& [entity, health] : *registry.GetComponentArray<Health>()) {
    health.current -= 1;
}

Over several components:

auto& positions = *registry.GetComponentArray<Position>();

for (auto& [entity, position] : positions) {
    if (!registry.HasComponent<Velocity>(entity)) {
        continue;
    }
    auto& velocity = registry.GetComponent<Velocity>(entity).value().get();
    position.x += velocity.x * dt;
    position.y += velocity.y * dt;
}

There is no hidden query language. The trade-off is a few HasComponent calls in exchange for data laid out contiguously.

docs.title: Destroying entities safely
docs.text:
Never call DestroyEntity() while iterating. Queue the destruction and let the frame finish:

if (health.current <= 0) {
    registry.QueueDestroyEntity(entity);
}

The queue is flushed at the end of the frame, after every system has run. Destroying a parent also destroys its descendants.

docs.title: Rendering systems
docs.text:
World-space renderers usually derive from LayeredRenderSystem instead of overriding Render directly. The renderer calls CanDraw() for every entity and then draws the matches sorted by Position::z, so sprites, shapes, and text can interleave correctly.

class HealthBarSystem : public Engine::LayeredRenderSystem {
  public:
    bool CanDraw(Engine::Registry& registry, Engine::Entity entity,
                 bool screenSpace) override {
        return !screenSpace && registry.HasComponent<Health>(entity);
    }

    void DrawEntity(Engine::Registry& registry, Engine::Entity entity) override {

docs.title: Add a camera
docs.text:
1. Create an entity.
  2. Add a CameraComponent with a follow target.
Engine::Entity camera = registry.CreateEntity();
Engine::CameraComponent cam;
cam.followTarget = player;
cam.followSpeed = 5.0f;       // 0 snaps instantly
cam.clampToBounds = true;
cam.bounds = {0.0f, 0.0f, levelWidth, levelHeight};
cam.zoom = 1.0f;
Engine::CameraPlugin::AttachToEntity(registry, camera, cam);

The camera is a normal entity: move it by moving its Position, rotate it via Rotation. Only one camera renders - the one with primary = true and the lowest entity id.

For shake, set cam.shakeTrauma = 1.0f; strength is shakeMagnitude * trauma^2 and trauma decays by shakeDecay per second. Shake is visual only.

Mouse input is in window pixels; convert with CameraSystem::ScreenToWorld before comparing to world positions.

See Engine → Rendering and Collisions for world vs. screen coordinates.

docs.title: Add a HUD
docs.text:
A HUD is drawn on top of the world, in window pixels, ignoring the camera.

  1. Create an entity and add a Text component.
  2. Add the ScreenSpace tag so it is drawn in the screen pass.
local hud = Entity.create()
Entity.setName(hud, "ScoreHUD")
Transform.setPosition(hud, 16, 16)
Component.addText(hud, "Score: 0", 24, 255, 255, 255, 255)
-- tag it ScreenSpace from C++ or via a prefab; in Lua you can store the entity id
-- and update the text each frame

Update the text every frame from your game script:

function Game:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    local score = self.score or 0
    -- find the HUD entity and update its text
    local hud = Entity.find("ScoreHUD")
    if hud then
        -- Text component has no Lua setter for the string yet; recreate or use a
        -- stored reference. For simple cases, keep the entity id in self.
    end
end

For a value that changes often, keep the entity id in self during onCreate and update its Text component from C++ or by recreating the entity. Sprites and shapes work the same way: anything tagged ScreenSpace is drawn in the screen pass.

See Engine → Rendering for the two-pass pipeline and Components → Text.

docs.title: Play a sound from Lua
docs.text:
Component.addAudioSource(entity, "assets/laser.wav", false, false, 1.0)
Component.playAudio(entity)

Or use the global Audio namespace:

Audio.playSound("assets/laser.wav", 1.0, false)

docs.title: Play music
docs.text:
Audio.playMusic("assets/music.mp3", 0.6, true)

Stop it with Audio.stopMusic("assets/music.mp3") or Audio.stopAllMusic().

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Sound effects are decoded into RAM and can overlap many times.
  • Music is streamed from disk with one playhead per asset.
  • Set loop = true for background tracks.
  • shouldPlay is cleared by AudioSystem after handling; set it once, not every frame.
  • Bundled ids are relative file names (laser.wav, not assets/laser.wav).

See Engine → Audio and Lua → Audio.

docs.title: Add multiplayer
docs.text:
Minimal checklist:

  1. Add a NetworkComponent to the entities you want replicated (usually on a prefab). Set authority: Server for enemies/pickups, Client for players, Shared for walls.
  2. Set syncTransform (and syncSprite if the sprite changes).
  3. Set prefabPath to the prefab the other side should instantiate.
  4. Guard simulation in scripts:
local function shouldSimulate()
    if not Net.isNetworked() then return true end
    return Net.isServer()
end

function Enemy:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    if not shouldSimulate() then return end
    -- move, animate, collide
end
  1. Launch with --server / --client, or use the editor's Play Multiplayer button.

Players are spawned by the engine from the Client-authority template's prefabPath; Lua cannot instantiate prefabs. Read a client's input on the server with Net.input(entity).

See Engine → Networking, Editor → Multiplayer, and Lua → Net.

docs.title: React to a hit in Lua
docs.text:
Connect the collision signal to a method on your script:

function Enemy:onCreate(entity)
    self.entity = entity
    Component.connect(entity, "onCollisionEnter", entity, "onHit")
end

function Enemy:onHit(selfEntity, other)
    log.info("hit by " .. tostring(other))
end

docs.title: Trigger zones
docs.text:
A collider with isTrigger = true reports overlaps without blocking. Use triggers for pickups, goals, and hit boxes:

Component.addBoxCollider(entity, 32, 32, true) -- isTrigger = true
Component.connect(entity, "onTriggerEnter", entity, "onPickup")

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Restrict what collides with what using layers and masks:

Component.setColliderLayer(entity, "Player")
Component.setColliderMask(entity, Layers.bit("Enemy") | Layers.bit("Wall"))

See Engine → Collisions, Lua → Collider, and Lua → Layers.

docs.title: Create an action
docs.text: Open Input Map from the menu bar. Type an action name (for example jump) and click + Add Action. Action names are case-sensitive: jump, Jump, and JUMP are three different actions.

docs.title: Bind keys
docs.text: Expand the action, click + Add Keybind, then click the Key button and press the desired key. You can bind several keys to one action (for example W and Up both map to MOVE_UP). You can also bind mouse buttons and gamepad buttons.

docs.title: Read the action in Lua
docs.text:
if Controller.isActionActive("jump", 1) then
    -- player 1 pressed jump
end

Player index defaults to 1. For local multiplayer, add a second player and read Controller.isActionActive("jump", 2).

docs.title: How it is stored
docs.text: The map is stored in the scene as m_InputMap and baked into the game launcher at build time. Changing it requires a rebuild before the game sees the new bindings.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Prefer action names over raw keys in scripts; rebinding then needs no code changes.
  • Use Controller.getActiveActions(playerId) to inspect what is currently held.
  • Custom devices: subclass IController and feed _activeActions from your source (network, AI, replay).

See Engine → Input, Editor → Input mapping, and Lua → Input & Controller.

docs.title: Gravity and jump
docs.text:
local Player = {}
local SPEED = 240
local GRAVITY = 900
local JUMP = -420

function Player:onCreate(entity)
    self.entity = entity
    self.vy = 0
    self.grounded = false
    Component.connect(entity, "onCollisionEnter", entity, "onCollisionEnter")
    Component.connect(entity, "onCollisionStay", entity, "onCollisionStay")
end

function Player:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    local dir = 0
    if Controller.isActionActive("left") then dir = dir - 1 end
    if Controller.isActionActive("right") then dir = dir + 1 end
    Transform.translate(entity, dir * SPEED * dt, 0)

    self.vy = self.vy + GRAVITY * dt
    if Controller.isActionActive("jump") and self.grounded then
        self.vy = JUMP
        self.grounded = false
    end
    Transform.translate(entity, 0, self.vy * dt)
end

function Player:onCollisionStay(selfEntity, other)
    self.grounded = true
end

return Player

docs.title: Animation (frame swap)
docs.text:
local frames = {"assets/p1.png", "assets/p2.png"}
local timer = 0
local frame = 1

function Player:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    timer = timer + dt
    if timer > 0.15 then
        timer = 0
        frame = (frame % #frames) + 1
        Component.setSpritePath(entity, frames[frame])
    end
    if Controller.isActionActive("left") then
        Component.setSpriteFlip(entity, true)
    elseif Controller.isActionActive("right") then
        Component.setSpriteFlip(entity, false)
    end
end

docs.title: Spawning with a timer
docs.text:
local EnemySpawner = {}
local timer = 0

function EnemySpawner:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    timer = timer + dt
    if timer > 2.0 then
        timer = 0
        local e = Entity.create()
        Entity.setName(e, "Enemy")
        Transform.setPosition(e, 900, 300)
        Component.addSprite(e, "assets/enemy.png")
        Component.addBoxCollider(e, 32, 32)
    end
end

return EnemySpawner

docs.title: Simple state machine in Lua
docs.text:
local Game = {}
Game.state = "menu"

function Game:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    if Game.state == "menu" then
        if Controller.isActionActive("start") then
            Game.state = "playing"
            Scene.load("levels/Level1.scene")
        end
    elseif Game.state == "playing" then
        -- gameplay
    elseif Game.state == "gameover" then
        if Controller.isActionActive("restart") then
            Game.state = "menu"
            Scene.load("levels/Menu.scene")
        end
    end
end

return Game

docs.title: Timers without blocking
docs.text:
Store a deadline and check it each frame; never use blocking waits.

self.deadline = Time.time() + 3.0

-- in onUpdate:
if Time.time() >= self.deadline then
    -- fire
    self.deadline = Time.time() + 3.0
end

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
A ScriptComponent points at a Lua file. The script must return a table. The engine calls, if defined:

  • onCreate(entity) - once, when the script is loaded.
  • onUpdate(entity, dt) - every frame, dt in seconds.
  • onDestroy(entity) - when the entity is destroyed.
  • onCollisionEnter/Stay/Exit(self, other) and onTriggerEnter/Stay/Exit(self, other) - when connected via Component.connect.

Each entity gets its own table, so self is never shared between entities. Store per-entity state on self in onCreate.

docs.title: Load order
docs.text: Scripts load during the game's first frames. ScriptSystem stays idle in the editor (the EditorMode resource is present), so Lua only runs in the game process started by Play.

docs.title: Auto-reload
docs.text: ScriptComponent.autoReload defaults to true and reloads the file when it changes on disk. There is no hot reload inside a running process: save the file, close the game window, and click Play again.

docs.title: Where logs go
docs.text: log.info, log.error, log.debug, and print write to the engine's log buffer. In the game process this appears in the terminal where you launched it (or the Console if launched from the editor, since build/play output lands there).

docs.title: Debugging tips
docs.text:
• If nothing happens, check that the game actually ran (click Play, then click the game window). The editor never runs Lua.
  • A Lua error prints to the log with the file and line; read the terminal/console.
  • Use log.info(tostring(value)) to inspect values.
  • Entity.find("Name") returns nil if no entity has that Name; guard with if.
  • Time.deltaTime() is a fallback 1/60; prefer the dt argument.
  • Scene.load is ignored on clients in multiplayer.

docs.title: What runs where (multiplayer)
docs.text: Call Server Client Single-player onCreate yes yes yes onUpdate (guarded by shouldSimulate) yes no yes Net.isServer() true false false Net.isNetworked() true true false Scene.load applies ignored applies Net.input(entity) for a player that player's input local player only controller input

docs.title: Spawn entities at runtime
docs.text:
From Lua, create a bare entity and dress it with components:

local e = Entity.create()
Entity.setName(e, "Bullet")
Transform.setPosition(e, x, y)
Component.addSprite(e, "assets/bullet.png")
Component.addBoxCollider(e, 8, 8, false, true) -- not a trigger, static-ish

Lua cannot instantiate a .prefab. For authored subtrees, spawn them from C++ or let the engine spawn them from a prefabPath in a NetworkComponent during replication.

When spawning many entities, queue destruction of the spawner's old instances with Entity.queueDestroy rather than Entity.destroy inside a loop.

See Lua → Entity and Editor → Prefabs.

docs.title: Switch scenes
docs.text:
From Lua:

Scene.load("levels/Level2.scene")

The switch happens at the end of the frame, after destruction is flushed. In multiplayer, only the server's Scene.load counts; clients ignore their own calls and follow the server.

From C++, use the SceneManager resource:

auto& scenes = registry.GetResource<Engine::SceneManager>();
scenes.RequestScene("levels/Level2.scene");

ClearEntities() removes all entities and restarts ids at 1, while keeping component types, systems, and resources registered.

See Engine → Application and Lua → Time, Scene, Log.

docs.title: Lua
docs.text:
Gameplay in Lucky & Pozzo is written in Lua. These pages document every namespace and function exposed to scripts, with exact signatures, return shapes, defaults, and gotchas.

  • Entity - create, destroy, find, name.
  • Transform - position, rotation, draw layer.
  • Component - sprites, shapes, text, colliders, opacity, hierarchy, connections, audio, scripts.
  • Input & Controller - keyboard, mouse, keybinds, actions.
  • Time - timing.
  • Scene - scene switching.
  • Log - logging.
  • Layers - collision layer names and masks.
  • Audio - global sound and music.
  • Net - multiplayer setup, messaging, replication, RPCs.

Conventions common to all pages:

  • Entity handles are plain numbers in Lua.
  • Most Component.* functions return bool success (false on missing component or dead entity).
  • Functions taking sol::optional arguments omit them as nil.
  • Transform.getPosition returns a fresh table {x, y, z}.
  • Component.getSprite returns the literal string "sprite" if a sprite exists, else nil; use getSpriteInfo for data.
  • log/print: print(...) converts each vararg to a string, joins with tabs, and logs via log_info. Non-string args throw.
  • Time.deltaTime() is a fallback constant 1/60; prefer the dt passed to onUpdate.
  • Scene.load is ignored on clients in multiplayer (the server drives scene changes) and errors if no SceneManager.
  • Component.has / remove / entitiesWith accept friendly alias names only: Position, Rotation, Sprite, Shape, Text, Name, Collider, Opacity, Parent, AudioSource.

See also: Engine → Lua scripting, Plugins → Lua plugins.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Extend the engine, the editor, or both. Plugins are the supported way to add behavior without forking.

  • Plugin lifecycle - Discovery, loading, initialization, and shutdown.
  • Engine plugins - Add systems, resources, and runtime services.
  • Editor plugins - Add panels, tools, and editor workflows.
  • Lua plugins - Write gameplay extensions in Lua.
  • Packaging plugins - Distribute plugins with a project or on their own.
  • Examples - Small plugins to copy from.

docs.title: Editor plugins
docs.text:
Engine plugins make a component run. Editor plugins make it editable: they tell the Inspector how to draw, add, and remove a component.

Without one, a registered component still shows up with a generic field editor. With one, you control labels, widgets, validation, and asset pickers.

docs.title: The IPluginEditor interface
docs.text:
#include "PluginEditor.hpp"

namespace Editor {
class IPluginEditor {
  public:
    virtual ~IPluginEditor() = default;
    virtual const char* GetName() const = 0;
    virtual const char* GetIcon() const = 0;
    virtual bool OnImGuiRender(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) = 0;
    virtual bool HasComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) = 0;
    virtual void AddComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) = 0;
    virtual void RemoveComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) = 0;
};
}

docs.title: A minimal editor plugin
docs.text:
#include "Components/Health.hpp"
#include "PluginEditor.hpp"
#include <imgui.h>

namespace Editor {
class HealthPluginEditor : public IPluginEditor {
  public:
    const char* GetName() const override { return "Health"; }
    const char* GetIcon() const override { return ICON_FA_HEART; }

    bool HasComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) override {
        return registry.HasComponent<Engine::Health>(entity);
    }

    bool OnImGuiRender(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) override {
        if (!HasComponent(entity, registry)) return false;
        auto& health = registry.RequireComponent<Engine::Health>(entity);
        ImGui::DragInt("Current", &health.current, 1.0f, 0, health.max);
        ImGui::DragInt("Max", &health.max, 1.0f, 1, 9999);
        ImGui::Checkbox("Invincible", &health.invincible);
        return true;
    }

    void AddComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) override {
        registry.AddComponent(entity, Engine::Health{});
    }

    void RemoveComponent(Engine::Entity entity, Engine::Registry& registry) override {
        registry.RemoveComponent<Engine::Health>(entity);
    }
};
}

docs.text:

#include "Plugins/HealthPluginEditor.hpp"
m_PluginEditors.push_back(std::make_unique<HealthPluginEditor>());

Order in the vector is the order of sections in the Inspector.

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Do not duplicate engine defaults. If the generic editor already shows the fields correctly, skip the plugin.
  • Use asset pickers for paths.
  • Clamp early; drag widgets can emit out-of-range values.
  • Keep serialization in sync: every field the inspector exposes must also be in ComponentReflect.hpp.
  • No logic here. The editor only writes component data; systems do the work.

docs.text:
An engine plugin registers components, systems, and resources behind one Init() call. The built-in plugins:

Plugin Registers PositionPlugin Position, PositionSystem RotationPlugin Rotation HierarchyPlugin Parent, HierarchySystem SpritePlugin SpriteComponent, SpriteSystem, AssetManager ShapePlugin ShapeComponent, ShapeSystem, plus OpacityPlugin TextPlugin Text, TextSystem CameraPlugin CameraComponent, CameraSystem ColliderPlugin ColliderComponent, CollisionEvents, CollisionSystem InputPlugin Input, InputManager AudioPlugin AudioSource, AudioSystem, AssetManager OpacityPlugin Opacity SignalPlugin SignalConnections ScriptPlugin ScriptComponent, ScriptSystem ReplicationPlugin NetworkComponent, ReplicationSystem MultiplayerPlugin PlayerInformation, network resources, MultiplayerSystem

ReplicationPlugin must register before MultiplayerPlugin. See Networking.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
class AudioPlugin : public Engine::IPlugin {
  public:
    void Init(Engine::Registry& registry) override {
        if (!registry.HasResource<Engine::AssetManager>()) {
            registry.AddResource<Engine::AssetManager>();
        }
        registry.RegisterComponent<Engine::AudioSource>();
        registry.RegisterSystem<Engine::AudioSystem>();
    }
};

Order inside Init(): resources first, then components, then systems. Guard shared resources with HasResource<T>().

docs.title: Plugin lifecycle
docs.text: A plugin is a C++ class implementing Engine::IPlugin. Its only method is Init(Registry&), called once during startup, before the first frame.

docs.title: Discovery and loading
docs.text: There is no dynamic loading. Plugins are compiled into the executable and instantiated in main() (or in the editor's RunEditor). Registration order is update order, so the order in which you call Init() matters.

docs.title: Initialization order
docs.text:
The generated game registers plugins in this order:

Engine::HierarchyPlugin hierarchy;
hierarchy.Init(app.GetRegistry());

Engine::PositionPlugin position;
position.Init(app.GetRegistry());

// ... sprites, shapes, text, rotation, replication, collider, opacity,
//     signal, input, audio, script, camera

HierarchyPlugin before PositionPlugin is required: hierarchy propagates parent motion, then position snapshots previous positions.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text: IPlugin has no shutdown method. Systems implement OnSceneUnloaded for per-scene cleanup. The Application destructor unloads the virtual resolution texture and closes the window.

docs.title: Lua plugins
docs.text: Lua scripts are the supported way to write gameplay without recompiling. A script returns a table with optional lifecycle functions and uses the engine's Lua API.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
local Enemy = {}

function Enemy:onCreate(entity)
    self.entity = entity
end

function Enemy:onUpdate(entity, dt)
    -- runs every frame
end

function Enemy:onDestroy(entity)
end

return Enemy

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Scripts can create and destroy entities, read and write components, query input, play audio, spawn prefabs indirectly through the engine, and call into the network API. They cannot instantiate .prefab files directly; the engine spawns those.

docs.title: Auto-reload
docs.text: ScriptComponent::autoReload (default true) reloads the script when the file changes. There is no hot reload in the running process; relaunch the game after saving.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: Ship scripts alongside the executable in the project's scripts/ folder. Paths in ScriptComponent are project-relative, so they resolve the same way in the editor and the built game.
